name: Serval and Kaitenzushi Buffet
description: Serval has just found a Kaitenzushi buffet restaurant. Kaitenzushi means that there is a conveyor belt in the restaurant, delivering plates of sushi in front of the customer, Serval. In this restaurant, each plate contains exactly $$$k$$$ pieces of sushi and the $$$i$$$-th plate has a deliciousness $$$d_i$$$. Serval will have a meal in this restaurant for $$$n$$$ minutes, and within the $$$n$$$ minutes, he must eat up all the pieces of sushi he took from the belt. Denote the counter for uneaten taken pieces of sushi as $$$r$$$. Initially, $$$r=0$$$. In the $$$i$$$-th minute ($$$1\leq i\leq n$$$), only the $$$i$$$-th plate of sushi will be delivered in front of Serval, and he can do one of the following: Take the $$$i$$$-th plate of sushi (whose deliciousness is $$$d_i$$$) from the belt, and $$$r$$$ will be increased by $$$k$$$; Eat one uneaten piece of sushi that he took from the belt before, and $$$r$$$ will be decreased by $$$1$$$. Note that you can do this only if $$$r \gt 0$$$; Or, do nothing, and $$$r$$$ will remain unchanged. Note that after the $$$n$$$ minutes, the value of $$$r$$$ must be $$$0$$$. Serval wants to maximize the sum of the deliciousnesses of all the plates he took. Help him find it out!
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$1\leq k \lt n\leq 2\cdot 10^5$$$) — the number of minutes of the meal and the number of sushi pieces in each plate. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_n$$$ ($$$1\leq d_i\leq 10^9$$$) — the deliciousness of each plate. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2\cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print a single integer — the maximum possible sum of the deliciousnesses of all the plates Serval took.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2085D — Serval and Kaitenzushi Buffet [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
